clinicalPearls: Presents as a well-demarcated, 'stuck-on' waxy or verrucous papule or plaque, most often on the trunk, face and scalp of middle-aged and older adults.
Colour ranges from pale tan through brown to almost black; heavily pigmented lesions on the face are a common source of melanoma referral.
Surface horn cysts (keratin-filled pseudocysts) and comedo-like plugged follicular openings are characteristic and best appreciated on dermoscopy.
Dermoscopic hallmarks include milia-like cysts, comedo-like openings, a cerebriform 'brain-like' pattern, fat fingers and sharply demarcated moth-eaten borders.
The dermatosis papulosa nigra and stucco keratosis variants represent phenotypic subtypes seen respectively in darker skin and on the distal lower limbs.
The sudden eruption of numerous lesions with pruritus (the sign of Leser-Trelat) may rarely signal an internal adenocarcinoma and warrants malignancy screening.
Irritated lesions can become inflamed, crusted and clinically alarming, mimicking melanoma or squamous cell carcinoma.
No treatment is needed for asymptomatic lesions; cryotherapy, curettage or shave excision are used for symptomatic or diagnostically uncertain lesions, with histology if malignancy is suspected.
reference.pathophysiology: Seborrhoeic keratoses are benign epidermal proliferations composed of monomorphous basaloid keratinocytes with variable squamous differentiation, forming acanthotic plaques containing horn cysts and pseudo-horn cysts. Activating somatic mutations in FGFR3 and in the PIK3CA gene are frequently identified, indicating clonal keratinocyte expansion, yet the lesions have negligible malignant potential. Accumulation of melanin within the proliferating keratinocytes accounts for the variable pigmentation. Their prevalence rises steeply with age and there is a clear familial predisposition, with ultraviolet exposure implicated in facial and truncal lesions.
additionalDifferentials: malignant melanoma (particularly heavily pigmented or irritated lesions)
additionalInvestigations: dermoscopy to identify milia-like cysts and comedo-like openings
shave or punch biopsy of atypical lesions
excisional biopsy with histopathology where melanoma cannot be excluded
screening for occult malignancy if the sign of Leser-Trelat is suspected
redFlags: rapid eruption of multiple lesions with pruritus (sign of Leser-Trelat) prompting a search for internal malignancy
asymmetry, irregular pigment network or ulceration suggesting melanoma
recent change in size, colour or bleeding within a pre-existing lesion
a solitary rapidly enlarging keratotic nodule raising concern for squamous cell carcinoma
reference.prognosis: Seborrhoeic keratoses are entirely benign with no intrinsic malignant potential, although individual lesions persist indefinitely and new ones accumulate with age. Recurrence after superficial removal is common if the lesion is incompletely destroyed.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing a heavily pigmented or irritated lesion as benign when it is actually melanoma, or vice versa, leading to inappropriate management.
Destroying a lesion by cryotherapy or curettage without histology when the clinical diagnosis is uncertain, thereby losing the specimen.
Overlooking the sign of Leser-Trelat and failing to investigate for an underlying adenocarcinoma.
Confusing a solitary lesion with a viral wart and applying inappropriate keratolytic treatment.
management: Reassure and observe, as lesions are entirely benign with no malignant potential
Remove symptomatic, irritated or cosmetically unwanted lesions by cryotherapy, curettage or shave excision, or electrocautery
Send tissue for histopathology whenever melanoma or another pigmented malignancy cannot be excluded
Take a diagnostic biopsy of atypical lesions rather than destroying them blindly
Investigate for an occult internal adenocarcinoma when a sudden eruption suggests the sign of Leser-Trelat
Advise that new lesions accumulate with age and that superficially treated lesions may recur
